title: Walk through what happens during exactly-once processing end-to-end (transaction coordinator, commit markers, producer ID/epoch fencing).
shortTitle: Walk through what happens during exactly-once processing end-to-end.

s1_definition.profdef: Exactly-once semantics in Kafka means that even with retries and failures, each input record affects the output and the consumer offsets exactly once, with no duplicates and no loss. It is built from three pieces: the idempotent producer, which uses a producer id and sequence numbers so the broker drops duplicate writes, Kafka transactions, which atomically commit the output records and the consumed offsets together under a transactional id managed by a transaction coordinator, and fencing by producer id and epoch, which disables a zombie old producer instance. Commit markers written to the partitions tell consumers which records belong to committed transactions.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a National Bank of India clerk who moves money and then records in the ledger that the job is done. Exactly-once is like a notarized atomic operation: either both the money movement and the ledger entry happen, or neither does, and if the clerk is replaced mid-task the old clerk's badge is revoked so he cannot sneak back and do the work twice. A special stamp on the ledger page says this block of entries is officially committed, and readers ignore any entries without that stamp.
s1_definition.oneliner: Exactly-once is idempotent writes plus a transaction that atomically commits output records and input offsets together, with a transaction coordinator, commit markers, and producer-id-and-epoch fencing stopping duplicates and zombies.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Exactly-once semantics in Kafka means that even with retries and failures, each input record affects the output and the consumer offsets exactly once, with no duplicates and no loss. It is built from three pieces: the idempotent producer, which uses a producer id and sequence numbers so the broker drops duplicate writes, Kafka transactions, which atomically commit the output records and the consumed offsets together under a transactional id managed by a transaction coordinator, and fencing by producer id and epoch, which disables a zombie old producer instance. Commit markers written to the partitions tell consumers which records belong to committed transactions.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a National Bank of India clerk who moves money and then records in the ledger that the job is done. Exactly-once is like a notarized atomic operation: either both the money movement and the ledger entry happen, or neither does, and if the clerk is replaced mid-task the old clerk's badge is revoked so he cannot sneak back and do the work twice. A special stamp on the ledger page says this block of entries is officially committed, and readers ignore any entries without that stamp.

**One line to remember:** Exactly-once is idempotent writes plus a transaction that atomically commits output records and input offsets together, with a transaction coordinator, commit markers, and producer-id-and-epoch fencing stopping duplicates and zombies.

sections.s2_technical:
The first piece is the idempotent producer, enabled with `props.put("enable.idempotence", "true")`. When enabled, the broker assigns the producer a unique producer id and the producer tags each record with a sequence number per partition. If a network hiccup causes the producer to resend a batch, the broker sees the same producer id and sequence number and silently drops the duplicate, so a retry does not create a second write. This alone gives exactly-once writes for a single producer session to a single partition.

The second piece is transactions, which extend idempotence across multiple partitions and tie the produce and the offset commit together. You set a stable `props.put("transactional.id", "settlement-tx-1")`, call `producer.initTransactions()` once, and then wrap work in `producer.beginTransaction()`, your sends, `producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, groupMetadata)`, and `producer.commitTransaction()`. The crucial part is `sendOffsetsToTransaction`: the consumer offsets are committed as part of the same transaction as the output records, so either both happen or neither does. This is what makes the classic consume-process-produce loop exactly-once.

The transaction coordinator is a broker-side component that manages each transactional id. It keeps the transaction state in an internal topic called the transaction log. When you commit, the coordinator writes commit markers, also called control records, into every partition the transaction touched, including the offsets topic. These markers are special records that are not business data; they tell consumers that the records before them in this transaction are now committed.

Producer id and epoch fencing handles zombies. When a producer with a transactional id calls `initTransactions()`, the coordinator bumps the epoch for that transactional id. If an old instance of the same producer, perhaps a hung process that everyone thought was dead, tries to write or commit with the old epoch, the coordinator rejects it with a producer-fenced error. This guarantees that only one live producer per transactional id can make progress, which prevents a zombie from committing stale work twice.

On the consumer side, exactly-once reads require `props.put("isolation.level", "read_committed")`. With this setting the consumer only delivers records that belong to committed transactions and skips records from aborted or in-flight transactions, using the commit markers to decide. If you left it as `read_uncommitted`, the consumer would see records that might later be rolled back.

A senior nuance is that exactly-once is end-to-end only within Kafka. The moment you write to an external system such as a database that is not part of the Kafka transaction, you either need that system to be idempotent or you need an outbox pattern, because Kafka cannot roll back a row you already inserted in PostgreSQL. Also, transactions add latency and coordinator overhead, so you use them where correctness truly demands it, like money movement, not for every topic.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs a settlement service that reads transfer requests from an input topic, computes the settled amounts, and writes settlement results to an output topic, then marks the input as processed. A duplicate settlement would move Rajesh's money twice, which is unacceptable.

Problem 1 — a network retry causes the producer to resend the settlement result, creating a duplicate. This is exactly what the idempotent producer with producer id and sequence numbers solves: the broker drops the duplicate write.

Problem 2 — the service writes the settlement result but crashes before committing the input offset, so after restart it reprocesses the same transfer and settles twice. This is exactly what a Kafka transaction solves: the output record and the input offset commit together atomically.

Problem 3 — a hung old instance of the settlement service wakes up and tries to commit stale work while a new instance is already running. This is exactly what producer id and epoch fencing solves: the coordinator has bumped the epoch, so the zombie is fenced out.

The code will show a consume-process-produce loop using a transactional producer with a transactional id, sending offsets inside the transaction, and committing atomically, with a read-committed consumer downstream.

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: broker1:9092
    producer:
      transaction-id-prefix: settlement-tx-   # enables transactions
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement-service
      enable-auto-commit: false
      isolation-level: read_committed          # only see committed records
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer request on `transfer-requests`, for example Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001), fifty thousand rupees, at offset 42.

Step 1 — on startup the producer calls `initTransactions()`. The transaction coordinator registers the transactional id and bumps its epoch, which fences any older instance still holding the previous epoch.

Step 2 — the consumer polls and reads the request at offset 42. The service opens a transaction with `beginTransaction()`.

Step 3 — the service computes the settlement result and sends it to `settlement-results`. Because idempotence is on, this write carries the producer id and a sequence number, so a retry cannot duplicate it.

Step 4 — the service calls `sendOffsetsToTransaction`, adding the input offset 43 (the next to read) into the same transaction. Now the output result and the input offset are bound together.

Step 5 — the service calls `commitTransaction()`. The coordinator writes commit markers into the `settlement-results` partition and into the consumer offsets partition. Both become visible atomically. If the service had crashed before commit, nothing would be visible and the request would be reprocessed cleanly.

Step 6 — a downstream consumer with read-committed isolation reads `settlement-results`. It only sees the result because the commit marker is present; had the transaction aborted, it would skip those records entirely.

```
2026-10-24 22:00:01 [INFO] Settled SAV2001 offset 42
2026-10-24 22:00:01 [INFO] Transaction committed (results + offsets atomically)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  transfer-requests / partition 0 / offset 42
    │
    ▼
  Consumer (read_committed) poll → request SAV2001→CUR3001 Rs.50000
    │
    ▼
  producer.initTransactions()  ──→ Transaction Coordinator
    │                               bump epoch → FENCE old instance
    ▼
  producer.beginTransaction()
    │
    ├─ send result → settlement-results (pid + seq# → idempotent)
    │
    ├─ sendOffsetsToTransaction({transfer-requests-0 : 43})
    │        (input offset joins the SAME transaction)
    ▼
  producer.commitTransaction()
    │
    ▼
  Coordinator writes COMMIT MARKERS into:
    ├─ settlement-results partition
    └─ __consumer_offsets partition
    │  (both visible atomically — or neither on abort)
    ▼
  Downstream Consumer (read_committed)
    only delivers records before a COMMIT marker; skips aborted
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Exactly-once processing in Kafka is built from three pieces. The first is the idempotent producer, which the broker gives a unique producer id, and every record carries a per-partition sequence number, so if a retry resends a batch the broker recognizes the same producer id and sequence number and drops the duplicate. That alone stops duplicate writes.

The second piece is transactions. I set a stable transactional id, initialize transactions once, and then wrap each unit of work in begin, send, send-offsets-to-transaction, and commit. The key move is sending the consumer offsets inside the same transaction as the output records, so the output and the input offset commit atomically. Either both become visible or neither does, which is what makes the consume-process-produce loop exactly-once. A broker-side transaction coordinator manages the transactional id in an internal transaction log and, on commit, writes commit markers into every partition the transaction touched, including the offsets partition.

The third piece is fencing by producer id and epoch. When a producer initializes transactions, the coordinator bumps the epoch for that transactional id, so if a hung old instance wakes up and tries to commit stale work, it is rejected with a producer-fenced error. On the reading side, I set the consumer isolation level to read-committed so it only delivers records from committed transactions and skips anything aborted or in flight.

In my National Bank of India settlement service, this guaranteed that a transfer was never settled twice even under retries, crashes, or a zombie instance. The important caveat I always mention is that exactly-once is end-to-end only inside Kafka. The moment we wrote to the external ledger database, we made that write idempotent or used the outbox pattern, because Kafka cannot roll back a row already committed in PostgreSQL.
